summary: Gustavo Gutierrez (1928-2024) was a Peruvian Dominican priest and theologian widely regarded as the father of Latin American liberation theology, whose book A Theology of Liberation (Teologia de la liberacion, 1971) framed theology as critical reflection on Christian praxis in the light of a 'preferential option for the poor' and understood salvation as including liberation from social, political, and economic injustice.
description:
Gustavo Gutierrez was born in Lima, Peru, in 1928, of partly Quechua descent, and after early studies in medicine and philosophy trained for the priesthood and studied theology in Europe (Louvain and Lyon) before returning to pastoral and academic work in Peru. He later entered the Order of Preachers (the Dominicans) and, in his final decades, taught at the University of Notre Dame in the United States. He died in Lima in 2024.

Gutierrez is regarded, on the standard account of the movement's historians, as the principal founder of Latin American liberation theology. He is credited with giving the approach its programmatic name and statement: from a 1968 lecture, later expanded into his best-known book, Teologia de la liberacion: Perspectivas (Lima, 1971; English, A Theology of Liberation, Orbis, 1973). In that work he presents theology, on his own account, not primarily as a body of doctrine but as 'critical reflection on praxis', that is, reflection on committed Christian action on behalf of the poor, carried out in the light of the word of God. Central to his thought is the 'preferential option for the poor', the commitment to read the gospel from the standpoint of the poor and oppressed and to make their liberation a first concern of Christian life and reflection; the phrase and its emphasis became, through his work and the 1968 Medellin conference of the Latin American bishops, one of the most widely discussed themes of twentieth-century theology. Gutierrez holds, on his own account, that salvation is not reduced to social or political liberation but includes it: he distinguishes levels of liberation (from unjust social structures, from all that dehumanizes, and from sin as the ultimate root), while insisting they are bound together in the one saving work of Christ. To analyze the situation of poverty and oppression, he and other liberation theologians draw on social-scientific tools, including categories drawn from Marxist social analysis such as class and structural injustice; on the movement's own account this is a tool of analysis rather than an adoption of Marxist philosophy or atheism.

Gutierrez's later writings develop the spirituality implicit in this theology, above all We Drink from Our Own Wells (Beber en su propio pozo, 1983) on the spiritual journey of a people, and On Job (Hablar de Dios desde el sufrimiento del inocente, 1986), a study of innocent suffering and the language of God. His work was engaged, and in part critiqued, by the Roman Catholic magisterium: the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith's 1984 Instruction Libertatis Nuntius warned against an insufficiently critical use of Marxist concepts in liberation theology while affirming the preferential option for the poor, and its 1986 companion Libertatis Conscientia set out a fuller account of Christian freedom and liberation. This entry records Gutierrez's theology as his own attributed position and records the magisterial reception as an attributed position too, adjudicating neither.
editorial_notes:
This entry presents Gustavo Gutierrez's theology as his own attributed position (neutrality #1, #2). His distinctive claims (theology as critical reflection on praxis, the preferential option for the poor, salvation as including but not reduced to social/political/economic liberation, the use of Marxist social analysis as a tool rather than a philosophy) are stated as his and the movement's own self-understanding, not endorsed or refuted.
